evidence.title: Generative AI's healthcare professional role creep: a cross-sectional evaluation of publicly accessible, customised health-related GPTs
evidence.outcome: Regulatory approval status of health-related GPTs in FDA, EU MDR and TGA databases
evidence.effect: None of 1,055 health-related GPTs were approved by FDA, EU MDR or TGA; 624 used healthcare professional titles in names or descriptions.
evidence.quote: None of the customised GPTs identified were FDA, EU MDR, or TGA-approved.
evidence.country: Not specified (OpenAI GPT store, international; regulatory databases US, EU, Australia)

commentary.bottom_line: Forty-five sources endorse screening AI tools for medical device or SaMD status before deployment, but no study tests whether such screening prevents deployment of unvalidated regulated tools. One descriptive audit found that none of 1,055 health-related GPTs held FDA, EU MDR, or TGA approval, which shows the hazard exists without showing that screening solves it.

perspectives.view: No study compares deployment outcomes with and without regulatory status screening. The one available study is a cross-sectional audit that documents the hazard, so it cannot inform the effect of the practice. The 45 endorsements reflect expert consensus and regulatory text, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence of benefit.

The audit found that 624 of 1,055 health-related GPTs used healthcare professional titles in their names or descriptions, and none held regulatory approval. This suggests unvetted tools may present themselves as clinical authorities. A pre-deployment screen may intercept such tools, but no study has measured how often screening catches them or whether harm declines.

Endorsing sources cite the EU AI Act classification of health AI as high risk and FDA draft guidance expecting verification and validation data in marketing submissions. The audit shows that general-purpose model products reach users outside FDA, EU MDR, and TGA pathways. SaMD status depends on intended use, so screening requires case-by-case review of how a tool will be used.

A patient who uses a GPT bearing a clinical title may assume someone has reviewed it, yet the audit found no approved tools among 1,055. Screening by a health system may protect patients within that system's services. It would not reach tools that patients find and use on their own.

commentary.research_gap: No study has evaluated an institutional process for classifying AI tools by device status. Useful studies would measure how many tools in current use lack required clearance, how consistently reviewers classify intended use, how often screening changes deployment decisions, and whether screened portfolios show fewer safety events than unscreened ones.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and the hazard study did not report the populations using the GPTs it audited. The evidence therefore says nothing about Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and it cannot show whether screening works in safety-net systems that may have fewer staff available for regulatory review.
